## Introduction

In this example, we use a discrete-time SIR model and Turing.jl to infer the susceptible population $N$, the transmission rate ($\beta$), recovery-rate parameter ($\gamma$), and the initial infected proportion ($\rho$) from line-list data. This dataset originates from a study conducted on the H1N1 outbreak at Washington State University (WSU) in 2009, recording the number of daily cases over a period of 105 days. The dataset was obtained from [KhudaBukhsh et al. (2019)](https://github.com/cbskust/SDS.Epidemic/tree/master). The original raw data only included daily counts of new infections; KhudaBukhsh et al.\ reconstructed individual infection times from those counts and generated individual recovery times by sampling from an exponential distribution with rate $\gamma$ fixed at $1/5.5$ per day, the mean of prior infectious-period estimates. The resulting dataset (WSU.csv) contains individual-level infection times (first column) and recovery times (second column) for 2,276 cases, including 10 individuals whose recovery occurred after the 105-day observation window and are therefore treated as right-censored.

## Utility functions

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

"""
Convert a rate to a probability over time t.
"""
@inline function rate_to_proportion(r, t=1.0)
    if r < 0 || isnan(r)
        return 0.0
    elseif isinf(r)
        return 1.0
    else
        result = 1 - exp(-r * t)
        return isnan(result) ? 0.0 : max(min(result, 1.0), 0.0)
    end
end

"""
Generate a vector of counts from a vector of times and the total number of timesteps.
"""
function time_counts(times::AbstractVector{<:Integer}, nsteps::Integer)
    counts = zeros(Int, nsteps)
    @inbounds for t in times
        1 ≤ t ≤ nsteps && (counts[t] += 1)
    end
    return counts
end

"""
Prepare real data from DataFrame for analysis.
"""
function prep_sds(df::DataFrame, Tmax)
    ti     = Float64[]
    delta  = Float64[]
    cens   = Bool[]
    for r in eachrow(df)
        t_inf, t_rec = r[1], r[2]
        t_inf ≥ Tmax && continue                # infection after cut-off - ignore
        
        # Calculate recovery interval
        recovery_interval = t_rec - t_inf
        
        # Only include valid recovery intervals 
        if recovery_interval > 0
            push!(ti, t_inf)
            if t_rec < Tmax                        # full recovery observed
                push!(delta, recovery_interval)
                push!(cens, false)
            else                                   # right-censored
                push!(delta, Tmax - t_inf)
                push!(cens, true)
            end
        end
    end
    return ti, delta, cens
end

"""
Load and prepare real epidemic data from WSU.csv file.
"""
function load_real_data(csv_file::String, Tmax::Float64)
    # Load the data
    df = CSV.read(csv_file, DataFrame)
    
    # Prepare the data 
    ti, delta, cens = prep_sds(df, Tmax)
    
    # Convert to appropriate format for analysis
    K = length(ti)  # Total number of infections
    
    # Convert infection times to discrete time steps 
    ti_discrete = clamp.(round.(Int, ti) .+ 1, 1, 1_000_000) #So day 0 isn't dropped
    nsteps = max(maximum(ti_discrete), 105) # 105 days of data
    
    # Create histogram of infection times
    th = time_counts(ti_discrete, nsteps)
    
    # Convert recovery intervals to integers (rounding to nearest day)
    delta_discrete = max.(1, round.(Int, delta))
    @assert sum(th) == K "sum(th) must equal K, check infection day discretisation"
    
    return Dict(
        :K => K,
        :ti => ti_discrete,
        :delta => delta_discrete,
        :th => th,
        :nsteps => nsteps,
        :cens => cens,
        :ti_original => ti,
        :delta_original => delta
    )
end
```

## SIR model

The model is a discrete-time SIR model with geometric recovery times. In this model we assume that the recovery time is the same for all individuals and that the recovery time is independent of the infection time. 

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

function sir_map!(du, u, p, t)
    (S, I, C, Y) = u
    (β, γ) = p
    infection = rate_to_proportion(β*I)*S     # New infections
    recovery = rate_to_proportion(γ)*I        # New recoveries
    @inbounds begin
        du[1] = S - infection                 # Update susceptibles
        du[2] = I + infection-recovery        # Update infected
        du[3] = C + infection                 # Update cumulative infections
        du[4] = infection                     # Store new infections
    end
    nothing
end

function solve_map(f, u0, nsteps, p)
    # Pre-allocate array 
    sol = similar(u0, length(u0), nsteps + 1)
    # Initialise the first column with the initial state
    sol[:, 1] = u0
    # Iterate over the time steps
    @inbounds for t in 2:nsteps+1
        u = @view sol[:, t-1] # Get the current state
        du = @view sol[:, t]  # Prepare the next state
        f(du, u, p, t)        # Call the function to update du
    end
    return sol
end

function simulate(β, γ, ρ, nsteps)
    tspan = (0, nsteps)
    u0 = [1-ρ, ρ, 0.0, 0.0] # Initial conditions: S, I, C, Y
    p = [β, γ]
    sol = solve_map(sir_map!, u0, nsteps, p)
    τ = sol[3,end]      # Final size (total infected)
    f = sol[4,2:end]    # New infections per time step
    f = abs.(f)         # Ensure non-negative values
    # Handle edge cases 
    if τ <= 0 || any(isnan.(f)) || any(isinf.(f))
        f = fill(one(eltype(f))/nsteps, nsteps)
    else
        f = f./τ         # Normalise frequencies
    end 
    return sol, τ, f
end
```

## Turing model

The Turing.jl probabilistic model used to infer the parameters from this dataset employs the previously defined discrete-time SIR model. 

The susceptible population $N$ is integer-valued and enters the likelihood only through the Binomial final-size term $K \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N, \tau)$. Instead of sampling it, we sum this term over its prior support $N \in \{K+1, \ldots, N_{\max}\}$ (`marginal_N_loglik`, from the shared `IntegerParameters.jl`). The discrete-time model and its likelihood are unchanged; only the remaining real-valued parameters $(\beta, \gamma, \rho)$ are sampled, with NUTS. Posterior draws of $N$ are recovered afterwards from its exact conditional distribution given $\tau$.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
@model function dsa_discrete_turing_multinomial_inferN(
                                   N_grid::NGrid,           # Prior support of N: DiscreteUniform(K + 1, N_max)
                                   nsteps::Int,             # Number of time steps
                                   K::Int,                  # Observed total infections
                                   th::Vector{Int},         # Histogram of infection times
                                   delta::Vector{Int},      # Observed recovery intervals
                                   cens::Vector{Bool})      # Censoring (true=right-censored)
    
    # Priors for model parameters (N ~ DiscreteUniform(K + 1, N_max) is summed out below)
    β ~ Uniform(0.01, 5.0)   # Transmission rate 
    γ ~ truncated(LogNormal(log(1/5.5), 0.3), 0.01, 1.0)   # Recovery rate 
    ρ ~ Beta(1.0, 10.0)      # Initial infected proportion: small seed (mean 0.09), allowing the substantial
                             # fraction implied by a mid-epidemic start
    
    # Simulate deterministic model 
    _, τ, f = simulate(β, γ, ρ, nsteps)
    
    # Ensure τ is valid for binomial distribution
    τ_valid = max(min(τ, 1.0), 0.0)
    
    # Ensure f is valid for multinomial distribution
    f_valid = max.(f, 1e-10)           # Add small positive value to avoid zeros
    f_valid = f_valid ./ sum(f_valid)   # Normalise
    
    # Likelihood for number of infections, summed over N:
    #   log Σ_N P(N) · Binomial(K; N, τ)
    Turing.@addlogprob! marginal_N_loglik(N_grid, τ_valid)
    
    # Likelihood for infection times 
    th ~ Multinomial(K, f_valid)
    
    # Likelihood for recovery times 
    ϵ = 1e-8
    pγ = rate_to_proportion(γ)
    pγ_valid = min(max(pγ, ϵ), 1 - ϵ)
    log_surv = log1p(-pγ_valid)
    # 1-indexed geometric, P(W = n) = pγ (1 − pγ)^(n−1) for n ≥ 1, matching the per-step
    # recovery probability of the SIR map (Distributions.Geometric itself starts at 0)
    G1 = LocationScale(1, 1, Geometric(pγ_valid))
    for i in eachindex(delta)
        if cens[i]
            Turing.@addlogprob!(delta[i] * log_surv)  # log P(W > delta[i]) = delta[i]·log(1 − pγ)
        else
            delta[i] ~ G1
        end
    end
    
    return τ_valid   # used to draw N after sampling
end
```

Model parameters:

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

N_max = 18000   # ≈ WSU student body (18,234 served by the campus health service; Vaidya et al. 2015)

th = real_data[:th]         # Infection times
K = sum(th)                 # Total infections
delta = real_data[:delta]   # Recovery intervals
cens  = real_data[:cens]    # Censoring
nsteps = real_data[:nsteps] # Number of time steps

N_grid = NGrid(K, K + 1, N_max)   # prior support of N, summed out in the likelihood
```

## Running the inference

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
model = dsa_discrete_turing_multinomial_inferN(N_grid, nsteps, K, th, delta, cens);

n_samples  = 2000
nuts_adapt = 1000
n_chains   = 4
sampler    = NUTS(nuts_adapt, 0.8; max_depth=12, Δ_max=1000.0)
# Chains start from jittered data-based values (Methods): γ from the mean recorded recovery interval
# (p_γ = 1/mean δ), β at R0 = 1 (N is unknown, so the final size cannot be used) and ρ at its prior median;
# each value is multiplied by exp(0.1 z), z ~ N(0, 1), per chain.
init_rng = Xoshiro(20261006)
function data_inits(n)
    pγ0 = 1 / mean(delta[.!cens]); γ0 = -log(1 - pγ0); ρh = median(Beta(1.0, 10.0))
    j() = exp(0.1 * randn(init_rng))
    [InitFromParams((β = j() * pγ0, γ = clamp(j() * γ0, 0.011, 0.99), ρ = j() * ρh)) for _ in 1:n]
end

_ = sample(model, sampler, 1; progress=false, chain_type=MCMCChains.Chains)

@time chain = sample(model, sampler, MCMCThreads(), n_samples, n_chains;
                     progress=false, chain_type=MCMCChains.Chains, initial_params=data_inits(n_chains));

# Posterior draws of N: one draw from P(N | K, τ) per MCMC draw, added to the chain as :N
τ_draws = returned(model, chain)
N_draws = [sample_N(N_grid, τ) for τ in τ_draws]
chain   = hcat(chain, setrange(Chains(reshape(N_draws, size(N_draws, 1), 1, :), [:N]), range(chain)));
```

Posterior summaries with 95% credible intervals. Derived quantities (R₀ and mean infectious period) are computed sample-by-sample from the chain.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

N_chain  = vec(chain[:N])
β_chain  = vec(chain[:β])
γ_chain  = vec(chain[:γ])
ρ_chain  = vec(chain[:ρ])
pγ_chain = rate_to_proportion.(γ_chain)

R0_chain       = β_chain ./ pγ_chain   # R0 of the discrete process = β / (1 - exp(-γ))
IP_steps_chain = 1 ./ pγ_chain         # mean infectious period in steps (geometric, the actual fitted process)
tau_chain      = K ./ N_chain          # observed attack rate posterior

function posterior_summary(x; digits=4)
    (median = round(median(x); digits=digits),
     mean   = round(mean(x);   digits=digits),
     q025   = round(quantile(x, 0.025); digits=digits),
     q975   = round(quantile(x, 0.975); digits=digits))
end

posterior_table = (
    N         = posterior_summary(N_chain; digits=0),
    β         = posterior_summary(β_chain),
    γ         = posterior_summary(γ_chain),
    ρ         = posterior_summary(ρ_chain),
    R0        = posterior_summary(R0_chain),
    IP_steps  = posterior_summary(IP_steps_chain; digits=2),
    K_over_N  = posterior_summary(tau_chain),
)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

for (name, s) in pairs(posterior_table)
    println(rpad(string(name), 10),
            "  median = ", s.median,
            "   mean = ",   s.mean,
            "   95% CI = [", s.q025, ", ", s.q975, "]")
end

# 90% credible intervals, for comparison with the 90% intervals reported by KhudaBukhsh et al. (2020, Table 4)
println()
println("90% credible intervals:")
for (name, v, dg) in (("N", N_chain, 0), ("β", β_chain, 4), ("γ", γ_chain, 4), ("ρ", ρ_chain, 4), ("R0", R0_chain, 3), ("IP_steps", IP_steps_chain, 2))
    println(rpad(name, 10), "  median = ", round(median(v), digits=dg), "   90% CI = [", round(quantile(v, 0.05), digits=dg), ", ", round(quantile(v, 0.95), digits=dg), "]")
end

println()
println("Convergence diagnostics:")
ess_summary = MCMCDiagnosticTools.ess(chain)
rhat_summary = MCMCDiagnosticTools.rhat(chain)
display(ess_summary)
display(rhat_summary)
```

end

## Comparison to KhudaBukhsh et al. (2019) results

We plot the S_t curve and the final epidemic size distribution to compare our observed and simulated data, with that obtained in KhudaBukhsh et al. (2019).

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

# Simulate with inferred parameters 
sol, τ_post, f_post = simulate(β_post, γ_post, ρ_post, nsteps)

# Extract susceptible population over time (scaled to inferred N̂)
S_traj = sol[1, :] .* N_post  # First row contains S values

# Calculate observed susceptible population over time
S_observed = zeros(nsteps + 1)
S_observed[1] = (1 - ρ_post) * N_post  # Initial susceptible

# Subtract cumulative infections at each time step
cumulative_infections = cumsum(real_data[:th])
for t in 1:nsteps
    S_observed[t + 1] = S_observed[1] - cumulative_infections[t]
end

# Create plot of susceptible population over time
p_susceptible = plot(0:nsteps, S_traj, 
                    label="Inferred", 
                    color=:blue, 
                    linewidth=3,
                    xlabel="Time", 
                    ylabel="Count of susceptibles",
                    title="S_t curve",
                    legend=:topright, 
                    grid=true)

# Add observed susceptible population
plot!(p_susceptible, 0:nsteps, S_observed, 
      label="Observed", 
      color=:red, 
      linewidth=3,
      linestyle=:dash)

display(p_susceptible)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

# Calculate final epidemic size from the MCMC samples
final_size_samples = Float64[]
for i in 1:length(chain[:β])  
    β_i = chain[:β][i]
    γ_i = chain[:γ][i]
    ρ_i = chain[:ρ][i]
    N_i = chain[:N][i]
    
    # Simulate with these parameters
    _, τ_i, _ = simulate(β_i, γ_i, ρ_i, nsteps)
    
    # Calculate final epidemic size in absolute numbers
    final_size = τ_i * N_i
    push!(final_size_samples, final_size)
end

# Create histogram of the final epidemic size distribution
p_final_size = histogram(final_size_samples, bins=100, alpha=0.7, 
                        label=false, 
                        color=:blue,
                        normalize=:pdf,  # This makes y-axis density
                        xlabel="Final size", 
                        ylabel="Density",
                        xlims=(2000, 2500),
                        title="Final epidemic size")

# Add vertical line for the mean
final_size_median = median(final_size_samples)
final_size_ci    = quantile(final_size_samples, [0.025, 0.975])
vline!([final_size_median], label="Median = $(round(final_size_median, digits=0))",
       color=:red, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dash)
vline!([K], label="Observed = $K",
       color=:green, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dot)

display(p_final_size)
```

## Manuscript figure export

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#| label: fig-h1n1

using Measures
using PGFPlotsX
# Render the saved PDF via LuaLaTeX so Unicode Greek glyphs (β, γ, ρ) are
# embedded correctly instead of being substituted with '?'. GR's PDF writer
# uses a bundled font without Greek; PGFPlotsX hands the figure to LaTeX,
# whose default Computer Modern fully supports Greek.
PGFPlotsX.latexengine!(PGFPlotsX.LUALATEX)
pgfplotsx()

let
    # Posterior predictive epidemic curve: simulate from sub-sample of chain
    n_draws    = min(500, length(β_chain))
    sample_idx = round.(Int, range(1, length(β_chain); length=n_draws))
    f_mat      = Matrix{Float64}(undef, nsteps, n_draws)
    for (j, i) in enumerate(sample_idx)
        _, τ_i, f_i = simulate(β_chain[i], γ_chain[i], ρ_chain[i], nsteps)
        f_mat[:, j] = f_i .* τ_i .* N_chain[i]
    end
    f_lower  = [quantile(f_mat[t, :], 0.025) for t in 1:nsteps]
    f_median = [quantile(f_mat[t, :], 0.50)  for t in 1:nsteps]
    f_upper  = [quantile(f_mat[t, :], 0.975) for t in 1:nsteps]

    # NOTE: we deliberately do NOT set `fontfamily` here. Setting it to a font
    # without Greek glyphs (e.g. Helvetica) makes β/γ/ρ/δ render as missing
    # boxes under both GR and pgfplotsx + LaTeX. Each backend's default font
    # (GR's bundled font; LaTeX's Computer Modern via pgfplotsx) supports Greek.
    default(guidefontsize  = 9,
            tickfontsize   = 8,
            legendfontsize = 7,
            titlefontsize  = 10,
            linewidth      = 1.5,
            framestyle     = :box,
            grid           = true,
            gridlinewidth  = 0.3,
            gridalpha      = 0.4,
            gridcolor      = :gray,
            gridstyle      = :dash)

    p_curve = bar(1:nsteps, real_data[:th];
                  label         = "Observed",
                  color         = :lightgray,
                  linecolor     = :gray,
                  linewidth     = 0.3,
                  bar_width     = 1.0,
                  xlabel        = "Day",
                  ylabel        = "Reported cases",
                  title         = "(A) Posterior predictive epidemic curve",
                  left_margin   = 6mm,
                  right_margin  = 3mm,
                  bottom_margin = 5mm,
                  top_margin    = 2mm)
    plot!(p_curve, 1:nsteps, f_median;
          ribbon    = (f_median .- f_lower, f_upper .- f_median),
          fillalpha = 0.4,
          fillcolor = :steelblue,
          lw        = 0,
          label     = "95% CrI",
          color     = :steelblue)
    plot!(p_curve, 1:nsteps, f_median;
          lw    = 2.5,
          label = "Posterior median",
          color = :steelblue)

    # Thousands formatter for the N axis (avoids overlapping scientific notation).
    fmt_thousands(x) = string(Int(round(x / 1000))) * "k"

    p_N = histogram(N_chain;
                    bins         = 40,
                    normalize    = :pdf,
                    color        = :steelblue,
                    label        = "",
                    xlabel       = "N",
                    ylabel       = "density",
                    title        = "(B) Susceptible population",
                    xformatter   = fmt_thousands,
                    left_margin  = 5mm,
                    bottom_margin= 5mm,
                    top_margin   = 2mm)
    p_β = histogram(β_chain;
                    bins         = 40,
                    normalize    = :pdf,
                    color        = :steelblue,
                    label        = "",
                    xlabel       = "β",
                    ylabel       = "density",
                    title        = "(C) Transmission rate",
                    left_margin  = 5mm,
                    bottom_margin= 5mm,
                    top_margin   = 2mm)
    p_γ = histogram(γ_chain;
                    bins         = 40,
                    normalize    = :pdf,
                    color        = :steelblue,
                    label        = "",
                    xlabel       = "γ",
                    ylabel       = "density",
                    title        = "(D) Removal rate",
                    left_margin  = 5mm,
                    bottom_margin= 5mm,
                    top_margin   = 2mm)
    p_ρ = histogram(ρ_chain;
                    bins         = 40,
                    normalize    = :pdf,
                    color        = :steelblue,
                    label        = "",
                    xlabel       = "ρ",
                    ylabel       = "density",
                    title        = "(E) Initial inf. fraction",
                    left_margin  = 5mm,
                    bottom_margin= 5mm,
                    top_margin   = 2mm)

    # Two-row layout: curve full-width on top, four histograms in a row below.
    l = @layout [a{0.50h}; grid(1, 4)]
    fig = plot(p_curve, p_N, p_β, p_γ, p_ρ;
               layout           = l,
               size             = (1400, 700),
               dpi              = 300,
               background_color = :white)

    figdir = joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "Discrete_DSA_manuscript", "figures")
    mkpath(figdir)
    out = joinpath(figdir, "fig_h1n1.pdf")
    savefig(fig, out)
    println("Saved -> $out")
    fig
end

# Restore GR as the default backend in case later cells or re-runs expect it.
gr()
```

## Discussion 

The analysis performed on the WSU H1N1 outbreak dataset from 2009 showed that the discrete SIR model, with geometric recovery times, captured the dynamics of the epidemic. The susceptible population $N$ has a posterior median of $11{,}664$ (95\% CI $[9{,}027,\,16{,}295]$), larger than the estimate of $7{,}051$ (90\% CI $[6{,}602,\,7{,}581]$) reported by KhudaBukhsh et al. (2020). The two analyses treat $N$ differently: here it enters through the Binomial final-size term and is summed out over a uniform prior, whereas KhudaBukhsh et al. impute it at each iteration as $n \sim \mathrm{NegBinom}(k, \tau)$ from the final-size equation and fix $\gamma^{-1} = 5.5$ days. The transmission rate ($\beta = 0.197$) and reproduction number ($R_0 = 1.01$, 95\% CI $[0.96,\,1.06]$) are close to theirs ($0.189$ and $1.06$), and the fitted mean infectious period ($5.12$ days) reproduces the mean recorded recovery interval.

This approach offers several advantages: a simple and interpretable modelling framework, fast computation and inference through Turing.jl, and clear parameter interpretation (transmission rate β, recovery rate γ, and initial infected proportion ρ). However, it's important to note that the model relies on key assumptions, including geometric recovery times and the modification of the original dataset to include recovery intervals, as the primary data only contained daily infection counts.
